subject: ela
skillName: Describe words and phrases in stories

items.prompt:
Read the poem below.

Green grass grows in the garden gate,
Glowing green from early to late.

Find the alliteration in this poem. Which words are part of it?
items.answer: The alliteration is the /g/ sound: green, grass, grows, garden, gate, glowing, green. Nearly every word in both lines begins with the letter G.

items.prompt:
Read the poem below.

I see the moon and the moon sees me,
The moon sees somebody I want to see.
God bless the moon and God bless me,
And God bless somebody I want to see.

What phrase is repeated in this poem?
items.answer: 'The moon sees' and 'God bless' are the key repeated phrases. 'I want to see' also repeats. The repetition makes the poem feel like a gentle chant or prayer.

items.prompt:
Read the poem below.

The cat sat on a mat so flat,
And that was that, and that was that.

Find all the rhyming words in this poem.
items.answer: 'Cat,' 'mat,' 'flat,' 'that' all rhyme. They all end with the -at sound.

items.prompt:
Read the poem below.

The candle flickers, faint and frail,
A tiny light against the gale.
It does not break, it does not fall,
The smallest light can save them all.

Find the alliteration and the rhyming pairs. Explain how each one adds to the poem's meaning about the candle.
items.answer: Alliteration: 'flickers, faint and frail' — the soft, fragile /f/ sounds match the weakness of the candle flame. Rhyming pairs: 'frail/gale' and 'fall/all.' The rhymes give the poem confidence: even though the candle sounds weak (frail), the rhyme 'gale' pairs it with the full force of the wind, and 'fall/all' pairs the candle's small light with the entire world it can save. The rhymes create a sense of balance and power that contradicts the candle's fragility.

items.prompt:
Read the poem below.

When I am brave, I climb the tree.
When I am brave, I cross the sea.
When I am brave, I face the night.
When I am brave, I find the light.

How does the repeated phrase 'When I am brave' structure the poem? What does starting each line the same way suggest about the speaker?
items.answer: Each 'When I am brave' acts as a condition, only when the speaker is brave can they do each extraordinary thing. The parallel structure suggests that bravery is not a permanent state but a choice made each time. The speaker is not always brave but in those moments when they are, anything becomes possible. The repetition also builds confidence — the list of brave acts grows, and so does the sense of who the speaker can be.

items.prompt:
Read the poem below.

Nadia noticed the night was near,
The neighbors' lamps were soft and clear,
And something in the evening light
Made everything feel warm and right.

Find the rhyming pairs and one example of alliteration. Explain how both contribute to the warm feeling of the poem.
items.answer: Rhyming pairs: 'near/clear' and 'light/right.' The /ear/ sound in 'near/clear' is gentle and soft, matching the soft lamplight. 'Light/right' ends the poem with a resolved, settled feeling. Alliteration: 'Nadia noticed the night' — the /n/ sound is quiet and close, like whispering, which creates a hushed evening atmosphere. Both tools reinforce the poem's tone of warmth and quiet comfort.

items.prompt:
Read the poem below.

We will plant the seed in the dark,
We will water it in the cold,
We will watch for the first small spark
Of something green and bold.
We will wait as the seasons turn,
We will trust what we cannot see.
We will learn what the seedlings learn:
That patience sets things free.

Analyze how the repeated 'We will' structure builds meaning across the whole poem. What does the shift from physical actions (planting, watering) to more abstract ideas (trust, patience) reveal about the poem's deeper message?
items.answer: The repeated 'We will' creates a collective, forward-looking voice — the speaker is not alone but part of a group committed to a shared effort. The first four uses describe physical actions: plant, water, watch. These are concrete, doable tasks. Then the poem shifts: 'We will trust what we cannot see' and 'We will learn what the seedlings learn' move from physical to emotional and philosophical. This shift reveals the poem's deeper message: tending a garden teaches you to have faith in invisible processes and to accept that growth happens on its own time. The final line, 'That patience sets things free,' is the wisdom earned by all the waiting.

items.prompt:
Read the poem below.

Owen stood at the ocean's edge
And made a quiet, personal pledge:
To carry some of this back home —
Not the water and not the foam,
But the way the horizon goes on
Long after you think it is gone.

How does the final image, 'the way the horizon goes on / Long after you think it is gone,' work as both a literal observation and a deeper idea? How do the rhyme and line break support the meaning?
items.answer: Literally, the image describes how the horizon seems to keep going no matter how far you look. Deeper, it suggests that some experiences, especially awe, beauty, or a sense of the infinite, cannot be contained. Owen is not taking water or foam (physical things), but a feeling or understanding. The rhyme 'gone/on' is placed across a line break: 'goes on' ends one line and 'Long after you think it is gone' begins the next, performing the very thing it describes. The poem goes on past where you thought it would end, just like the horizon. The structure enacts the meaning.
